title: Epigenome Alterations and 3D Chromatin Architecture Remodeling in Inflammatory Macrophage Activation under Diabetic Conditions
authors: Reddy, M. A.; Bhattacharya, S.; Tanwar, V. S.; Malek, V.; Chen, Z.; Zhang, L.; Lanting, L.; Wu, X.; Grant, M. B.; Tompkins, J.; Chen, Z. B.; Natarajan, R.
abstract: Aberrant monocyte/macrophage activation in diabetes drives chronic inflammation and diabetic complications. Although epigenetic mechanisms are implicated in these processes, the contribution of three-dimensional (3D) chromatin reorganization remains unclear. Here, we use integrated multi-omics approaches to profile gene expression, chromatin accessibility and 3D chromatin architecture in human CD14 monocyte-derived macrophages exposed to high glucose and TNF- (HT), mimicking the diabetic milieu. HT induces inflammatory transcription programs that recapitulate those observed in diabetes and dynamically remodel chromatin accessibility, enhancer-promoter interactions, and topologically associated domains. Inflammatory genes exhibit increased chromatin accessibility, whereas cell cycle and metabolic genes display reduced accessibility and weakened enhancer-promoter interactions. These architectural changes promote the convergence of lineage-determining and signal-dependent transcription factors at enhancer-promoter loops, generating distinct regulatory hubs that orchestrate pro-inflammatory responses. Similar enhancer-promoter interactions are observed in peripheral blood derived monocytes from individuals with diabetes. Furthermore, perturbing chromatin interactions via CRISPR interference targeting HT-induced enhancers suppresses nearby CCL2 and other chemokine genes. Collectively, this first comprehensive enhancer connectome map of macrophages under diabetic conditions advances the field by revealing extensive disease-associated rewiring of the 3D epigenome, highlighting chromatin architecture and epigenetic mechanisms as potential therapeutic target for diabetes-associated inflammation.

title: Spontaneous slow waves index multiple dimensions of recovery in Disorders of Consciousness
authors: Ruyant Belabbas, A.; Boullet, A.; Manasova, D.; Le Coz, A.; Valente, M.; Lejeune, F.-X.; Sitt, J. D.; Naccache, L.; Rohaut, B.; Andrillon, T.
abstract: Whether and how residual awareness is expressed in patients with Disorders of Consciousness (DoC) depends on the severity of brain damage and the transient functional state of the cortex at assessment. Classically, DoC are associated with electroencephalographic (EEG) slowing, marked by high-amplitude slow waves, even during the day. Yet, slow waves are also a hallmark of healthy sleep, where they are thought to serve restorative functions and to help maintain network homeostasis. Here, we asked whether slow waves in DoC can provide insights into the severity of cortical dysfunction or, conversely, into the preservation of residual awareness and recovery potential, by characterizing their spatial, temporal and morphological properties. We analyzed 256-channel EEG recorded during the Local-Global auditory paradigm in 236 DoC patients, including 123 in Unresponsive Wakefulness Syndrome (UWS), 62 in a Minimally Conscious State minus (MCS-) and 29 in MCS plus (MCS+). High-amplitude slow waves were detected as local events, and their density, amplitude and slopes were quantified scalp-wide and channel-wise, by mean level and temporal variability across the recording. Slow-wave features were related to concurrent (Coma Recovery Scale-Revised - CRS-R, Local-Global paradigm) and follow-up (one-year Glasgow Outcome Scale-Extended - GOS-E) assessments of consciousness and functional recovery. Associations with MRI-derived measures of cortical integrity and structural connectivity, and differences between anoxic and traumatic etiologies, were also examined. Slow waves were more frequent in less severe DoC patients (i.e., MCS) compared to UWS. Slow-wave slopes were also steeper frontally and increased at a faster rate in patients exhibiting higher levels of consciousness and/or markers of conscious access during the Local-Global paradigm. More frequent and steeper slow waves at baseline further predicted recovery of consciousness and of functional independence at one year. At the individual level, slow-wave features classified states of consciousness above chance (AUC = 0.62 and 0.71 for MCS- and MCS+ versus UWS), whereas outcome prediction remained modest (0.56-0.58). These clinical associations had a structural basis: slow-wave occurrence was greater after traumatic than anoxic injury and scaled with the integrity of subcortico-cortical projection fibers and consciousness-related cortical networks. Contrary to the classical view of delta activity as a non-specific marker of impaired consciousness, prominent spontaneous slow waves indexed behavioral and neurophysiological signs of awareness and better recovery. Beyond reflecting a propensity for pathological bistability, they may also signal the integrity of the networks required to generate them, together with their residual capacity for dynamic regulation.

title: Task demands shift motor learning from adaptation to feedback control in an unconstrained bimanual task
authors: Varghese, R.; Rossi, C.; Malone, L. A.; Bastian, A. J.
abstract: Bimanual actions are common in daily life, yet how task demands shape reliance on learning and control mechanisms remains largely unknown. We examined this in 73 participants who lifted a plate in virtual reality while we distorted visual motion of their right hand. During right-hand-only lifting, aftereffects were present but incomplete. Bimanual lifting with the same right-hand perturbation shifted learning further from adaptation toward feedback control: participants developed compensatory hand adjustments and showed smaller aftereffects. Relaxing precision demands improved success but neither restored aftereffects nor reduced compensation. Removing interlimb conflict by perturbing both hands did not improve success but eased compensatory adjustments and restored plate aftereffects to unimanual levels. Success rate during learning did not correlate with aftereffects, but faster movement speed did. This demonstrates that precision demands and interlimb conflict independently shift learning strategy in bimanual contexts.

title: Hippocampal extracellular matrix remodeling and temporally distinct glial reorganization following peripheral injury
authors: Ge, C.; Kausar, V.; Xu, L.; Maghsoudi, A.; Shtudland, G.; Amrami, M.; Betancourt, M.; Niaz, A.; Zirkiyev, J.; Alvarado, S. G.; Abzalimov, R.; He, Y.; Tajerian, M.
abstract: Chronic pain is frequently accompanied by anxiety and other affective disturbances, but the molecular and cellular changes linking peripheral injury to persistent alterations in brain function remain incompletely defined. The hippocampal extracellular matrix (ECM) regulates synaptic plasticity, cellular signaling, and neuroimmune interactions and may therefore contribute to pain-related central plasticity. We used a tibial fracture/cast immobilization model to examine temporal changes in hippocampal ECM, glial morphology, and affective behavior following peripheral injury. Behavioral testing was performed at 3, 7, and 20 weeks after injury, while high-dimensional morphometric analysis of microglia and astrocytes was performed at 1, 3, 7, and 20 weeks. Hippocampal ECM associated molecular signals were mapped at the chronic stage using decellularization coupled with MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry imaging. Injured mice developed mechanical hypersensitivity and reduced exploration in two anxiety related paradigms during the early and chronic stages, with these behavioral phenotypes no longer detected at 20 weeks. At 7 weeks, injury was associated with changes in hippocampal ECM-associated peptide signals, including reduced signals corresponding to four ECM-associated proteins. Microglia and astrocytes exhibited distinct, time-dependent changes in density and multidimensional morphology, with some alterations persisting after behavioral measures returned toward control levels. In vitro, BV2 microglia exhibited rigidity-dependent changes in morphology, phagocytic behavior, and calcium signaling. Together, these findings define a temporally evolving hippocampal ECM and glial phenotype following peripheral injury and identify matrix biomechanics as a candidate regulator of microglial function.

title: Immediate cortical responses to transcranial magnetic stimulation of the human motor leg area
authors: Beck, M. M.; Nuyts, M.; Sakalauskaite, L.; Rothwell, J.; Siebner, H. R.; Christiansen, L.
abstract: Background: Immediate transcranial evoked potentials (iTEPs) are ultra-early electroencephalographic responses elicited by single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) of the primary motor cortical hand area (M1-HAND). Their characteristic latency, waveform, and sensitivity to short-interval intracortical inhibition suggest a close relationship to the cortical generators of indirect corticospinal volleys (I-waves). Here, we tested the hypothesis that iTEPs constitute a fundamental physiological response of human motor cortex and therefore generalize across motor representations, including the leg representation (M1-LEG). Methods: Single-pulse TMS was delivered over the motor cortical representation of the right tibialis anterior (TA) in 16 healthy volunteers. In a subset of participants (n=10), stimulus-response curves and paired-pulse short-interval intracortical inhibition (SICI) measures were obtained. Results: TMS of M1-LEG elicited reproducible iTEPs consisting of a slow positive deflection with superimposed high-frequency peaks with topographic maxima in electrodes adjacent to the stimulation site. M1-LEG iTEPs emerged close to active motor threshold and increased in prevalence and amplitude with increasing stimulation intensity. Paired-pulse stimulation produced consistent SICI of the second and third iTEP peaks. M1-LEG stimulation also evoked conventional later TEPs with latencies and polarities closely resembling those recorded after M1-HAND stimulation. Conclusions: TMS of the human M1-LEG elicits robust iTEPs that closely resemble those recorded from M1-HAND in their timing, intensity dependence, and sensitivity to intracortical inhibition. These findings indicate that iTEPs are not specific to M1-HAND but reflect a general physiological response of human motor cortex closely linked to corticospinal I-wave generation. This broadens their utility as a non-invasive probe of excitatory and inhibitory circuit dynamics throughout the human motor system.

title: Aging reshapes odor-evoked dynamics in central olfactory circuits
authors: Chapman, I. F.; Bolding, K. A.
abstract: Olfactory decline is among the earliest signs of aging and predicts later cognitive decline and neurodegenerative disease. Age-related impairments in odor identification and discrimination implicate central olfactory brain regions in both mice and humans, but it remains unclear where in the processing hierarchy aging alters neural function relating to these cognitive and perceptual deficits. To resolve this, we acquired simultaneous Neuropixels recordings from olfactory bulb (OB) and piriform cortex (PCx) in young and old mice during awake, head-fixed odor presentation, allowing us to probe multiple levels of odor response features within each animal. Our recordings revealed a shift toward greater excitation in both regions and reduced inhibitory neuron activity in PCx. Aging also restructured odor-evoked local field potential (LFP) oscillations within and across regions, with strongly elevated beta power and coherence. Population odor representations were less discriminable in OB, but not in PCx. Thus, our results point to reduced discriminability of OB population odor representations as the clearest neural analog of previously reported discrimination deficits. Single-unit, LFP, and population measures did not collapse onto a single axis using dimensionality reduction, indicating that several partly independent processes reshape the dynamics of odor responses in central olfactory circuits with aging. Together, these findings identify central circuit excitation/inhibition (E/I) and oscillatory imbalances that parallel age-related olfactory dysfunction despite largely preserved odor responsivity.

title: Model-based pupil deconvolution reveals latent attentional dynamics
authors: Maity, S.; Mathot, S.; Ray, S. B.
abstract: Changes in pupil size have been widely used as an indirect measure of attention. However, attention engages on a faster timescale than the pupillary response. Therefore, the slow time course of the pupil response makes it difficult to distinguish attentional responses to stimuli presented in close temporal succession. Although signal deconvolution has been used in previous research to estimate latent attentional responses from the pupil signal, existing methods primarily model dilation without considering the visual stimulus evoked constriction phase of the pupil. Here, we introduce a dual-kernel deconvolution model that models constriction and dilation using separate impulse response functions. Using an RSVP paradigm with emotional faces as target stimuli, we demonstrate that the proposed model estimates latent attentional response despite substantial overlap in the measured pupil signal. Importantly, the recovered attentional response resembles the time course of attentional allocation previously predicted by several models of Attentional Blink. Together, these findings demonstrate that the dynamics of latent attentional episodes can be recovered from the pupil response with a temporal resolution previously obscured by the sluggishness of the pupillary response. The proposed method is also provided as a usable software package that serves as a general tool for investigating the temporal dynamics of attention in rapid visual paradigms.

title: Eyes on the prize: a neural basis of perceptual choking under pressure
authors: McDonnell, M. E.; Chandrasekaran, A. N.; Ki, C. S.; Smoulder, A. L.; Miyata, H.; Yu, B.; Batista, A. P.; Smith, M. A.; Chase, S. M.
abstract: Even professional athletes sometimes fail to perform when it matters most. This phenomenon, known as choking under pressure, has been observed in a variety of motor and cognitive tasks. Can inordinately large rewards influence even sensory processing, and if so, what might be its neural basis? To probe this, we studied rhesus monkeys performing a challenging color change detection task and recorded from populations of neurons in visual area V4. We found that monkeys underperformed when offered rare "jackpot" rewards and uncovered associated detrimental alterations in V4 population activity. These findings were consistent with misallocated spatial attention, providing a potential neural basis for perceptual choking under pressure.

title: Biophysical modeling of excitation/inhibition imbalance in Alzheimer's disease
authors: Deng, Q.; Chen, C.; Zikopoulos, B.; Yazdanbakhsh, A.
abstract: INTRODUCTION: Alzheimer's disease (AD) involves early sensory and perceptual changes that can precede memory decline. We developed a two-layer rate-based neural model of early and higher visual areas with feedforward, feedback, and recurrent connections to examine how excitatory/inhibitory (E/I) balance shapes visual motion perception in AD. METHODS: Using Motion-Induced Position Shift and Altered Motion Repulsion stimuli, we factorially manipulated excitatory (E) and inhibitory (I) subfield power and connectivity to examine their effects on illusion representation across visual layers. RESULTS: Increased E, decreased I, and increased E/I reduced illusion representation, consistent with reduced illusion susceptibility in AD, whereas the converse increased illusion representation, reflecting neurotypical processing. Higher-level layer 2 representations were more resistant to E/I perturbations than lower-level layer 1. Illusion representation was less affected by E/I increases in intra-areal (recurrent) connectivity than in inter-areal (feedforward/feedback) connectivity. DISCUSSION: This mechanistic framework links E/I balance and connectivity to altered visual motion illusion representations in AD and suggests that E/I and connectivity measures may provide probes of early AD neurobiology. The framework may also generalize beyond vision.

title: Retinotopic organization of head-orienting vectors in the pigeon ventral lateral geniculate nucleus
authors: Severin, D.; Reynaert, B.; Vega-Zuniga, T.; Letelier, J. C.; Marin, G.; Karten, H. J.; Mpodozis, J.
abstract: The ventral lateral geniculate nucleus (GLv) is a conserved retinorecipient structure positioned between visual and premotor systems, yet its role in visuomotor transformations remains poorly understood. Here, we examined whether the pigeon GLv contains a spatially organized motor representation linking visual-field locations to orienting movements. Anatomical tracing identified descending projections from neurons in the GLv inner lamina (GLv-li) through pretectal and tegmental regions toward pontine targets. GLv-li projection neurons are GABAergic, yet electrical microstimulation of GLv-li in awake pigeons evoked rapid head movements followed by smaller eye movements. Each stimulation locus produced a reproducible characteristic motor vector whose direction and duration were largely insensitive to stimulation parameters, whereas movement amplitude and velocity approached site-specific plateaus. Movements initiated from different head positions were better explained by repetition of a fixed displacement than by convergence toward a common spatial goal. Critically, motor-vector direction was systematically related to the direction of the visual receptive field represented at the same GLv locus, while motor-vector amplitude covaried with receptive-field eccentricity. These defining features persisted after optic tectum ablation. Together, these findings reveal a retinotopically-organized map of fixed-vector head movements in the avian GLv and identify a tectum-independent route through which visual spatial representations can access descending orienting circuitry.

title: Focal drug uncaging for the precise control of endogenous nicotinic receptors in behaving mice
authors: Guyon, N.; Mohayyaei, M.; Bergel, A.; Grellier, G.; Jehl, J.; Pietrancosta, N.; Rebola, N.; Francois, A.; Faure, P.; Ellis-Davies, G. C. R.; Mourot, A.
abstract: Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors shape diverse brain functions, including reward, aversion, and pain, but dissecting their roles in vivo requires drug delivery with spatiotemporal precision that conventional pharmacology cannot provide. Here we establish in vivo photopharmacology of endogenous nicotinic receptors: two complementary, highly-potent agonists, administered systemically in an inactive caged form, are photoreleased locally in target brain circuits of behaving wild-type mice. Despite irreversible photochemistry, photoactivation can be repeated over many trials on a minute timescale, for hours following a single injection. Local uncaging evokes circuit-specific dopamine release, drives place preference from the ventral tegmental area and aversion from the interpeduncular nucleus, and, in pain circuits, reveals a pronociceptive effect masked when the same agonists are given systemically. By controlling where and when nicotinic signaling acts, this approach exposes circuit-specific drug effects invisible to conventional pharmacology, and outlines a general strategy for on-demand control of endogenous receptors in vivo.

title: Synaptic density imaging associates with performance but not self-report in autism
authors: Naples, A. J.; Cayir, S.; Cukar-Capizzi, C.; Wolf, J. M.; Mcclelland, J. E.; Robertson, E. C.; Sawant, S. S.; Matuskey, D.; McPartland, J. C.
abstract: Autism is a common neurodevelopmental condition with considerable between-person variability and unknown biological etiology. Diagnosis of autism in adults relies on measurement of performance (e.g., clinician rating of social behavior, standardized assessment of cognition) and self-report of autism features. Our prior work revealed a strong relationship between clinician ratings of social function in autism and in vivo measures of synaptic density as measured by [11C]UCB-J PET (Matuskey et al., 2025). However, it is not understood how the measured aspects of the autism phenotype index underlying biology. Here, in a sample of 12 autistic adults, we address this question by relating synaptic density imaging to a range of performance measures, such as cognition and face recognition, in contrast to self-report measures. Our results identify a dissociation between these measurement types in that synaptic density correlates strongly with measures of performance but shows virtually no relationship with self-report. These findings suggest that, while self-report and performance measures share variance in characterizing phenotypes in autism, they diverge when mapping onto the underlying biology. Results suggest that higher synaptic density may index a general mechanism that facilitates social and cognitive performance across a range of tasks. These data also indicate that performance and self-report measures are not interchangeable in capturing brain-behavior correspondences in autism, a finding that can guide measure selection in future biomarker studies and clinical research.

title: Impaired astrocytic Cx43 syncytial network in lateral habenula affects synaptic connectivity and drives adolescent stress-induced depression
authors: Li, H.; Wang, Q.; Su, Y.; Chen, H.; Wu, Z.; Chen, X.; Wang, C.; Zhao, Y.; Li, D.; Huang, X.; Fu, R.; Huang, W.; Tang, Y.; Niu, J.; Verkhratsky, A.; Yi, C.
abstract: Adolescent depression is a major neuropsychiatric disorder induced by early life stress; the underlying cellular mechanisms instigating pathological circuit malformation remain unclear, and, consequently, effective therapeutic strategy is limited. Here, we analysed the contribution of astrocytes to early life stress-induced adolescent depression using a mouse model of parental separation. We identified a previously unrecognised regional specialisation of lateral habenula (LHb) astrocytes, characterised by compact cellular domains, abundant leaflets, and enhanced Cx43 gap junctional coupling. Parental separation selectively reduced astrocytic Cx43 expression and gap junctional communication in the LHb, which was accompanied by profound astrocytic atrophy and loss of leaflets. Single-cell sequencing further revealed that parental separation induces a broad reorganisation of LHb astrocyte transcriptional states, including metabolic, stress-response, and inflammatory programs; moreover, it specifically reduces astrocyte-neuron communication. Consistent with this, we found that structural remodelling of LHb astrocytes affected tripartite synapse geometry, resulting in impaired excitatory and inhibitory synaptic transmission, and neuronal Ca2+ hyperexcitability, all ultimately associated with depressive-like behaviours. Selective knockdown of astrocytic Cx43 in the LHb recapitulated these pathological changes and translated into depressive-like behaviours. Mechanistically, we found that impaired Cx43 gap junctional communication is associated with excessive astrocytic Ca2+ dynamics, resulting in Rac1-GTPase activation and decreased p-Ezrin levels. In vivo inhibition of LHb astrocytic Ca2+ signalling rescued astrocytic atrophy and depressive-like behaviours following parental separation. Together, our findings establish a Cx43-Ca2+-Rac1-p-Ezrin pathway that links gap junction malfunction to structural remodelling of astrocytes and disruption of neuron-astrocyte interactions in the developing LHb. Our study reveals astrocytic Ca2+ dysregulation as an active downstream effector of Cx43 dysfunction and identifies a regionally specialised astrocytic mechanism through which early-life stress disrupts synaptic transmission and neuronal function during adolescence, providing a potential cellular target for intervention in adolescent depression.

title: Design and Test Novel EEG Electrode Attachments for Type 4 Afro-textured Hairstyles
authors: Broor, M.; Ogunniyi, K.; Williamson, L.; Liu, C.
abstract: Black participants remain underrepresented in electroencephalography (EEG) research, partly because current EEG devices work poorly with dense, coily Type 4 Afro-textured hair. Research-grade EEG typically wires electrodes on a cap, and therefore the electrodes often fail to reach the scalp through dense, Afro-textured hair. Protocols that ask Black participants to unbraid or restyle protective hairstyles add burdens that discourage enrollment in research studies. To address this, we designed and tested 3D-printed attachments that fit onto an EEG electrode and anchored it directly in the hair, using the hairstyle itself as the mounting structure. We fabricated three design configurations for natural Afro-textured hair, cornrows/braids, and twists/microlocs. Seventeen healthy adults with Type 4a-4c hair used electrode attachments that matched their hairstyle. During a single visit, EEG was recorded with 16 conventional cap electrodes defined by the international 10-20 system and with 16 electrodes using novel electrode attachments anchored directly to their hair. Participants completed resting and walking trials with each system. Electrode-to-scalp distance and gel volume were measured during setup. Electrode disconnection, impedance, signal quality (i.e. peak alpha power and aperiodic (1/f) component), and comfort level were measured throughout the data collection. Compared with the conventional cap, the novel attachments reduced electrode-to-scalp distance, gel use, and impedance. Twenty percent of the conventional cap electrodes failed to connect to the scalp compared with 0.1% of novel electrodes. Impedance rose across trials for the conventional cap, whereas the novel attachments showed a smaller increase and maintained lower impedance throughout. Signal quality was significantly better using the novel attachments, while comfort level did not differ between systems. In conclusion, hair-anchored electrode attachment may present a feasible alternative to conventional cap-based EEG for people with Type 4 hair, yielding more usable channels and better signal quality, and supporting more inclusive EEG acquisition.

title: Dorsomedial striatal Bmal1 deletion in medium spiny neurons alters EPSCs and dendritic morphology after chronic exposure to alcohol in female mice.
authors: Darvishmolla, M.; Courtemanche, R.; Amir, S.; Chapman, A.
abstract: Circadian clock genes in the striatum modulate alcohol drinking behavior in female mice, but the underlying synaptic mechanisms remain unknown. Medium spiny neurons (MSNs) of the striatum express D1- or D2-type dopamine receptors, which are differentially modulated by alcohol. Here we used whole-cell patch-clamp recordings to examine how deletion of the clock gene Bmal1 affects spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic currents (sEPSCs) in electrophysiologically identified D1 and D2 neurons of the female mouse dorsomedial striatum (DMS). Prior intermittent access to alcohol increased sEPSC amplitude in putative D1 neurons of wildtype mice without affecting sEPSC frequency, and this increase was accompanied by greater dendritic branching and complexity in biocytin-filled D1 MSNs. Bmal1 knockout had the opposite effect in D1 neurons, reducing sEPSC amplitude in both alcohol-exposed and alcohol-naive animals. In D2 neurons, alcohol produced only a non-significant trend toward increased sEPSC amplitude in wildtype mice, but a significant increase in Bmal1 knockout mice. Thus, local disruption of Bmal1 appears to block the alcohol-induced enhancement of sEPSCs in D1 neurons while unmasking a similar enhancement in D2 neurons. These findings may help explain how Bmal1 deletion in the DMS reduces alcohol consumption in female mice.

title: Cross-Tissue Inflammatory Convergence Supports a Putative Muscle-Brain Axis in Alzheimer's Disease
authors: Zhang, A.; Shen, W.; Yan, S.; Chen, J.; Liu, X.; Zou, J.; Li, S.; Hu, S.; Liu, Y.; Pan, C.; Lan, Z.; Peng, G.; Zhang, Q.; Peng, W.; Ahmadizar, F.; Zhang, J.
abstract: Background Reduced muscle strength is associated with cognitive decline and Alzheimer's disease (AD), suggesting that skeletal-muscle aging and AD-related neurodegeneration may share biological mechanisms. Vascular dysfunction, immune activation, and extracellular-matrix remodeling have been implicated in both tissues, but the extent of shared cellular and molecular programs remains unclear. We investigated cross-tissue transcriptional programs in aging skeletal muscle and AD-related brain tissue and evaluated whether related signals are detectable in peripheral blood. Methods We analyzed independent, unpaired human transcriptomic datasets from skeletal muscle (23 donors), the SEA-AD middle temporal gyrus atlas (84 donors), and peripheral blood. Donor-aware models identified age-associated changes in muscle and transcriptomic changes across continuous pseudoprogression score (CPS) in brain. Cross-tissue comparisons focused on 30 brain donors within an early CPS window. Shared tissue-derived programs were assessed in peripheral blood mononuclear cells and independently tested in frailty bulk-blood and Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) whole-blood datasets. CellOracle simulations were used to prioritize candidate transcriptional regulators. Results Aging muscle showed increased inflammatory, extracellular-matrix, and stromal communication programs. During early AD-related brain progression, vascular and immune populations showed increasing inflammatory and matrix-associated activity together with shifts in intercellular communication. Cross-tissue analysis identified six concordantly enriched pathways comprising 109 leading-edge genes in endothelial populations and four pathways comprising 51 genes in myeloid populations. Related peripheral-blood signatures varied across cohorts and cell types. However, in independent frailty and ADNI mild cognitive impairment and AD datasets, 23 of 30 predefined tissue-derived pathway-subset tests showed significant positive enrichment after false-discovery-rate correction, whereas individual gene-level bulk-blood associations did not survive correction. CellOracle analyses prioritized ETS2 and BHLHE40 as exploratory endothelial regulators whose simulated perturbation consistently reduced selected shared program scores across tissues. Conclusions Aging skeletal muscle and AD-related brain tissue exhibit convergent endothelial and myeloid inflammatory programs, with related pathway-level signals detectable in peripheral blood. These cross-tissue programs and candidate endothelial regulators provide testable hypotheses for mechanisms linking systemic aging, muscle dysfunction, and AD-related neurodegeneration.

title: Bone regulates locomotion by sustaining motoneuronal mitochondrial function
authors: Romeo Guitart, D.; Tirani, T.; Milunov, D.; Torres-Juacida, A. K.; Lamotte, B.; Arenas-Plascencia, C.; Durand, S.; Nemazanyy, I.; Moriceau, S.; Saha, S.; Karsenty, G.; Oury, F.
abstract: Body-brain communication is crucial for optimal neuronal performance across the lifespan, yet whether peripheral organs regulate spinal cord motoneuron (MN) function through circulating molecules remains unknown. The expression of hormone receptors by spinal MNs raises the possibility that circulating cues allow the spinal cord to sense the body's energetic state and sustain motor activity. Here, we show that the bone-derived hormones osteocalcin (OCN) signals on spinal MNs via its receptor GPR158. GPR158 is selectively enriched in spinal cholinergic MNs, and its loss, globally or specifically in spinal MNs, or the one of OCN, impairs locomotor function and reduces choline acetyltransferase (ChAT) levels. Mechanistically, OCN signaling through GPR158 fine-tunes autophagy, mitophagy and mitochondrial activity in spinal MNs. Restoring any of these processes, by pharmacologically inducing mitophagy or chemogenetically activating mitochondria, is sufficient to rescue the locomotor deficits of Gpr158-deficient mice. Finally, OCN restoration in aged mice reverses age-related locomotor decline through a mechanism that requires MN autophagy and mitophagy. This study reveals that through OCN, the skeleton influences motor functions by fine-tuning motoneuronal mitochondria, and suggests that age-related motor decline is, at least in part, reversible.

title: Neural Evidence of Early Sensitivity to Text in Pre-reading Toddlers
authors: Kherbawy, N.; Potter, C. E.; Jaffe-Dax, S.
abstract: Learning to read leads to widespread changes in brain organization, but it is not yet known when text first becomes a privileged stimulus. To test whether neural sensitivity to text can appear prior to reading instruction, 31 monolingual toddlers in Israel (2.1-3.6 years) not yet enrolled in school were presented with displays of real, native text and visually matched non-text symbols. Using functional near-infrared spectroscopy, we found different patterns of activity in response to text vs. non-text across multiple cortical regions. Most notably, text elicited more activity in the ventrolateral prefrontal cortex, a region often associated with language processing. These results suggest that through implicit sensitivity to regularities in their input, toddlers may be able to discover that text is a meaningful stimulus and could begin to develop associations that will allow them to build connections between language and text.

title: The Effective Visual Acuity of Butterflies in Flight
authors: Supple, J. A.; Li, W.; Ilic, M.; Kos, M.; Lin, H.-T.; Belusic, G.; Krapp, H. G.
abstract: The spatial visual acuity of an eye is determined by both the spatial sampling density of the retina and the angular sensitivity of individual photoreceptors. In insect compound eyes, these are respectively characterised by the interommatidial angle, {Delta}{varphi}, and photoreceptor acceptance angle, {Delta}{rho}. During movement, however, finite photoreceptor integration times cause retinal image motion to broaden the effective acceptance angle, potentially degrading spatial resolution beyond its anatomical limit. This problem is especially acute in flying insects, which experience large rotational velocities during locomotion and must actively stabilise gaze to limit retinal image motion. Butterflies present a particularly demanding case because their flight is characterised by large, wingbeat-coupled thoracic oscillations. Here, we quantify how gaze stabilisation limits motion blur in freely flying Monarch butterflies Danaus plexippus by combining free-flight kinematic reconstruction of the head and thorax with separate intracellular measurements of photoreceptor acceptance angles and integration times from quiescent butterflies. We found that, without head compensation, thoracic oscillations would broaden the effective photoreceptor acceptance angle from its quiescent value of 2.17{degrees} to 9.38{degrees} during take-off. Compensatory head movements substantially reduced this motion-induced broadening, limiting the effective acceptance angle to 5.28{degrees}. Nevertheless, this 2.4-fold broadening of effective photoreceptor acceptance angle represents a substantial degradation of spatial acuity in flight, highlighting motion blur as an important constraint on the visual ecology of flying butterflies.

title: Reduction of complex dynamic touch information to a single stable perceptual feature
authors: Zamani, N.; Stephens-Fripp, B.; Tymms, C.; Chan, S.; Pardakhtim, R.; Culburtson, H.; Hartcher-O'Brien, J.
abstract: Dynamic touch requires the perceptual system to extract stable material properties from complex, evolving signals. Here, we examine potential material property features for a constrained dynamic-touch regime: brief taps, in which contact-induced vibratory transients are prominent and sustained deformation cues are reduced. Using a spectral-energy compensation method, we conducted five psychophysical experiments in two degraded-feedback scenarios: soft finger interfaces, in which fingertip stiffness was reduced by an inflatable silicone bubble, and compliant-surface interactions, in which participants tapped foam surfaces. Participants made explicit hardness judgments in two-alternative forced-choice tasks and identified rendered materials in multi-alternative matching and classification tasks. Under these tapping-based conditions, judgments scaled systematically with total spectral energy and were largely independent of waveform family. When spectral energy and dominant-frequency cues were placed in conflict, classifications predominantly followed spectral energy. These results identify total spectral energy as a robust cue for hardness judgments and material identification from brief taps, rather than as a complete account of hardness perception across all exploratory procedures. The findings provide a compact rendering principle for haptic interfaces in which contact-triggered vibrotactile feedback is available.

title: Voluntary engagement predicts recovery across rehabilitation time points after experimental spinal cord injury
authors: Griffin, J. M.; Papaioannou, P.; Menon, R.; Cheyne, O.; Kellaway, S.; Svirskis, D.; Jutzeler, C.; Aziz, A.; Bradke, F.
abstract: Rehabilitation is the cornerstone of clinical care following spinal cord injury (SCI) and is frequently incorporated into preclinical studies to evaluate emerging therapies. However, the variables that influence the effectiveness of rehabilitation interventions in rodent models remain poorly characterized, limiting the translational value of preclinical research. Here, we performed a meta-analysis of 150 preclinical studies comprising more than 3000 rodents and 292 effect sizes to identify such factors associated with successful rehabilitation after SCI. Rehabilitation improved functional outcomes across multiple behavioral domains, with larger effects observed in thoracic than cervical injury models. Meta-regression identified environmental enrichment as the most effective strategy, particularly when combined with task-specific training. Longer rehabilitation duration was associated with improved recovery, whereas greater daily exposure to forced rehabilitation was associated with smaller gains. In contrast, prolonged access to voluntary rehabilitation did not show this relationship. Rehabilitation improved outcomes when initiated at all time points after injury, with greater benefits when initiated during the late subacute and intermediate phases. Rehabilitation approaches associated with higher stress burden produced reduced benefits, suggesting that stress may limit rehabilitation-induced recovery. Collectively, these findings identify rehabilitation type, duration, and delivery context as important determinants of recovery after SCI and support a broad therapeutic window for intervention. Our results favor low-stress, voluntary rehabilitation strategies that promote sustained engagement and provide principles for designing effective and biologically appropriate rehabilitation strategies, potentially improving translational success for emerging SCI therapies. One Sentence SummarySustained voluntary rehabilitation promotes functional recovery across stages of experimental spinal cord injury, whereas prolonged forced training may reduce its benefits.

title: Intracranial electrophysiology reveals distinct neural representations of nociception and salience in the human brain
authors: Joshi, S.; Polat, M.; Pantis, S.; Garg, R.; Ahmed, S.; Huang, Y.; McGeoch, P. D.; Keller, C. J.; Buch, V. P.; Mackey, S.; Parvizi, J.; Ramayya, A. G.
abstract: Neuroimaging studies have shown close overlap between neural representations of nociceptive stimuli and non-nociceptive, salient stimuli (such as low-probability sounds), leading to the proposal that nociception and salience share a common neural substrate in the human brain. Here we use high-resolution intracranial recordings from 13 neurosurgical patients (2,018 total electrodes) to show that neural representations of nociception and salience are anatomically and functionally distinct in the human brain. 77% of 107 electrodes that encoded nociceptive stimuli did not encode low-probability sounds ("nociceptive representations"), whereas 23% encoded both nociceptive and low-probability sounds ("salience representations"). Nociceptive representations were distinct from salience representations in terms of anatomical prevalence (posterior insula, inferior parietal, and perirolandic cortex vs. anterior insula, thalamus, and inferior frontal gyrus), timing (nociception preceded salience by 120 ms on a trial-by-trial basis), and function (intracranial electrical stimulation was more likely to cause sensory experience when applied near nociceptive representations, as compared to salience representations). These results provide strong evidence that nociception and salience have distinct neural substrates in the human brain, and that selective measurement of these distinct processes may help understand patient-to-patient variability in chronic pain and develop personalized brain stimulation treatments.

title: Acceleration of vision changes object representations from infancy to adulthood
authors: Spriet, C.; Serraille, E.; Naderi, S.; Agrebi, M.; Bouyahia, Z.; Derrode, S.; Kaiser, D.; Papeo, L.; Hochmann, J.-R.
abstract: While much of the neural and cognitive machinery for visual perception is in place within weeks from birth, we identified and quantified a fundamental difference between infant and adult vision: the temporal rate at which meaningful visual information can be reliably extracted. Using frequency-tagging electroencephalography with rapid serial visual presentation, we found that object categorization at 4 and 9 months is respectively seven times and two to three times slower than in adults. Using quantitative information from infants experiments, we created and presented accelerated visual streams to adults, to match infants perceptual experience. We used deep convolutional neural networks to identify object representations that match those elicited in adults when accelerating the information flow. Results show that acceleration compromises finer-grained object distinction while sparing broad, general object representations. We propose that slow vision is a design feature of early development for preserving and highlighting the most stable and general features of the world.

title: Larger Pre-Speech Auditory Modulation Is Associated With Smaller Corrective Responses To Auditory Errors
authors: Basciano, A.; Chao, S.-C.; Rogalsky, C.; Daliri, A.
abstract: PurposeDuring speech planning, the brain predicts the auditory consequences of its movements and modulates the auditory system--a process called pre-speech auditory modulation (PSAM). We investigated the link between PSAM and behavioral error correction and determined how aging influences these mechanisms. MethodsSeventeen young adults (18-32 years) and 13 older adults (50-85 years) performed a speaking task involving auditory feedback perturbations and a silent reading control. We measured electrophysiological responses (N1/P2) to auditory probes during speech planning and correlated these modulations with the magnitude of participants subsequent behavioral corrective responses. ResultsBoth groups showed significant modulation of N1 and P2. However, N1 modulation correlated with corrective responses only in young adults. Older adults showed reduced behavioral corrections and smaller, delayed P2 components. Despite these age-related behavioral differences and the loss of the modulation-correction correlation, older adults maintained modulation magnitudes comparable to those of younger adults. ConclusionsN1 modulation serves as a neural index of the brains predictive processes during speech planning. Aging appears to selectively disrupt the integration of these signals into motor output rather than the internal generation of the predictions themselves.
